## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro, Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle, Technical Lead | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 (Draft) | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. Seven per-origin connection pools were written to address part of this (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The missing error handling persists and compounds. It was found by chance in one of the only three server-side integration touchpoints that exist today, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring as the remaining systems are built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation identified and raised for correction (§7). 3. The present failure behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. *(Source: MRT Overview, opening constraint statement.)* | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. *(Source: MRT Overview, Bundles.)* | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. *(Source: MRT Overview, Projects and Organizations.)* Seven environments are in use: the six deployment tiers plus one ad-hoc test environment *(verified in Runtime Admin, 12 Aug 2026)*. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** *(Source: MRT Overview, App Server and Rendering constraints.)* | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. *(Source: `.docs/prd/regional.md`; `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5 Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture.)* | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts share a **single first-party origin** (AU at the root, the other seven path-prefixed); the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. *(Sources: `architecture.md` §Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope; MRT Overview, Environments constraints.)* | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual *(Source: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §9 Performance Strategy; summarised in `.docs/architecture.md` > Pre-Build Decisions #3.)* Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | ### 2.2 Assumptions | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and the number of integration modules the single application carries. | | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing deploy pipeline (one workflow per tier: dev, test, sit, uat, stg, prod), version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound operation in any integration blocks every other concurrent request on that process (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A: Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A: Single MRT application, with per-integration safeguards in the server-side layer.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes gaps that are real and demonstrated: integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, three route handlers leave work unobserved, and no upstream call carries a timeout short enough to fail before MRT's own execution ceiling does. Option A is therefore recommended **with safeguards**: one bundle, but with each integration confined to its own module, given its own connection pool with an independent connection cap and timeout budget, wrapped in its own error boundary, and with every route registration observing the promise it starts. These are specified in §5. Adopting Option A without them would settle the topology question while leaving the isolation gap open, which is the state this document exists to close. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: anyone who needs deploy or variable access for one integration necessarily has it for all of them. The platform provides no way to scope either within a single project. Accepted; revisit if the team composition changes such that per-integration scoping becomes necessary. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the gaps in §1.2 undefined. **Every file listed below is Tier 1**, so the implementing ticket must secure approval before starting. `config/`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and the `overrides/app/ssr/` modules all sit under Runtime & Integration Config, owner Integration / SI Partner (`frozenFiles.md`); `.claude/rules/` sits under Governance, requiring both squad leads and the Integration lead. Two of them, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `config/default.js`, are additionally **absolute** Tier 1 under Hard Rule #4 (§2.1), where the verified-session exception does not apply. At merge time `CODEOWNERS` routes all of these paths to the single `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` team, so there is one review gate but two owner conversations. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the **entire** promise chain it starts, not merely its final call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Three routes do not do this today (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure, or an invalid SLAS callback token, currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Two origins have hostnames that are still unconfirmed and carry TODOs: `sfccPaymentsPool` and `booxiPool`. Separately, six of the seven pools fall back to a literal placeholder string if their environment variable is unset, so confirm each is populated per tier. Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. **Also: `undici` is imported here but is not a declared dependency**; it resolves only transitively via `jsdom`. Declaring it requires integration-team approval under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #7, which is a prerequisite for this work, not a detail. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` inside `jwksCaching()`, currently a bare global-dispatcher call. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the `fetch` inside `paymentMetadataHandler()`. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on both `fetch` calls inside `sendMarketingCloudEmail()` (token exchange, then email send). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` is **absolute Tier 1** | Attach a `.catch()` to the **whole promise chain** in the passwordless-login and reset-password callback routes. Neither route observes anything today. Note the chain begins with `validateSlasCallbackToken`, which throws on an invalid or expired token (`slasTokens.ts:33,51`), so a fix that wraps only the inner `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)` call would still leave the auth path failing silently. Also observe the `jwksCaching(...)` call in the JWKS route. Three route registrations currently leave a promise unobserved. | Modified | | `config/default.js` is **Tier 1** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```javascript // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries, origins and connection caps are defined in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 and are deliberately not restated here, to avoid two copies drifting apart. Those caps are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. **What the pools add.** Node's `fetch` already creates a separate connection pool per upstream origin by default: it is backed by `undici`, whose `Agent` keys one `Pool` per origin. (Confirmed empirically against the Node 24 runtime rather than by reading a bundled copy, since Node's internal `undici` is not the one resolvable in `node_modules`.) A slow integration therefore does not starve an unrelated one, and that is not what explicit pools are for. What the default does **not** provide is a bound on how many connections a single origin may open, or a response timeout short enough to fail before MRT's execution ceiling. Explicit pools add exactly those two things: a **bound** per origin, so one integration under load cannot consume unbounded sockets or overwhelm its upstream, and a **timeout** that lets the integration fail cleanly and return an error rather than the platform terminating the whole request. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, so the integration returns an explicit error instead of the whole request being terminated by the platform. | Error | | An integration issues a burst of upstream calls | Its own pool caps the concurrent connections, so the burst queues within that integration rather than opening unbounded sockets and pressuring process file descriptors or the upstream itself. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation, per the constraint in §2.1. | Edge case | | SLAS callback validation (`jose` fetches the JWKS itself, `slasTokens.ts:38`) | Also outside this pattern: `jose` uses Node's `https.get` rather than `fetch`, so it takes no `dispatcher` (it accepts an `http.Agent` instead). It is not unprotected, however: it applies its own 5s `timeoutDuration` and caches the key set for 10 minutes (`cacheMaxAge`), with a 30s floor on forced reloads after a key miss (`cooldownDuration`), so it is low-frequency and already bounded. Left as-is; revisit only if those defaults prove unsuitable. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4 criterion 3. Three tests exist and pass today (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`). The table adds one further row that is deliberately not yet written because it depends on §5, and one recording why no E2E coverage applies. | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Unit / Integration | Asymmetric error handling across the real modules: `sendMagicLinkEmail` and `paymentMetadataHandler` run concurrently against the same upstream failure. | Currently: `sendMagicLinkEmail` rejects out of its module uncaught, while `paymentMetadataHandler` catches its own failure and still responds. After §5: both catch at their own boundary and return an explicit outcome. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Once §5 is implemented: that each pool's connection cap is actually enforced under load, and that its timeout fires before MRT's execution ceiling. Note this deliberately does **not** test cross-origin isolation, which §5.3 shows already holds by default. | Concurrency against one origin stays at or below its configured cap; a hung upstream fails through the pool's own timeout and returns an error, rather than running out MRT's 20s/16s ceiling. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is already gated in CI. ### 6.2 Regression Risk The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and Marketing Cloud email, all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The three tests above cover the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap or timeout tuning, which is why the load-test row is listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. One factor usefully bounds the blast radius of both: a `dispatcher` is passed per call site, so only the four SSR `fetch` calls listed in §5.2 change behaviour. Everything else, including all commerce traffic issued through `commerce-sdk-react`, is untouched by definition. --- ## 7. Risks & Mitigations | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation | Owner | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | §5 is never implemented, leaving Option A endorsed but its isolation gap open, the state this TSD exists to correct. | **High** | Raise the §5 work as its own ticket at sign-off and sequence it **before** the bulk of integration build-out. It is cheap now and grows more expensive per integration added. | Technical Lead / Squad A | | The module contract in §5.3 is not followed by future integrations, since nothing enforces it. The gap was originally introduced this way. | **High** | Document the contract as a rule in `.claude/rules/`, add it to the PR checklist, and consider an ast-grep or lint rule matching a `fetch(` in `overrides/app/ssr/` with no `dispatcher` key. | Squad A | | A future integration proves genuinely CPU-bound or requires process isolation, which Option A cannot provide at any level of implementation quality. | Low | Host that integration's layer **outside** MRT (general-purpose cloud compute, or a vendor-hosted API per Salesforce's Connected App pattern) and call it from the single app over HTTP via its own pool. Reassess if it arises. | Technical Lead | | Connection-pool caps in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 are derived from expected, not observed, concurrency and may be wrong under real traffic. | Med | Validate against per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics in the Stage load-test pass (§9.3 of that document) and revise before go-live. | Squad A / Integration | | Every file in §5.2 is Tier 1, spanning two owners (Integration / SI Partner, and Governance for `.claude/rules/`), with two of them additionally absolute under Hard Rule #4. Adding `undici` as a declared dependency needs integration-team approval under Hard Rule #7. The implementing ticket can stall awaiting these. | Med | Identify both owner conversations and the dependency approval when raising the ticket, so they run in parallel from the start rather than surfacing one at a time mid-implementation. `CODEOWNERS` routes every path to one team at merge, so the merge gate itself is single. | Technical Lead | | MRT proxy configuration and the bundle's `config/default.js` are independent sources of truth for the same routing and can silently drift. | Med | Treat the pair as a single change unit in the integration checklist; verify both when adding any proxy. | Squad A / Integration | | `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 justifies the connection pools as preventing one integration from exhausting connections for unrelated origins. Measurement (§5.3) shows Node isolates per origin already, so anyone re-deriving the caps from that rationale starts from a false premise. | Med | Correct the wording in all three copies: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §12.1, `.docs/architecture.md` > Blast-Radius Mitigation (which carries the same sentence and a duplicate of the same 7-pool table), and the published Confluence counterpart. The pools are still required, for the bounding and timeout reasons in §5.3, so no change to this TSD's recommendation. | PWA TSD owner | | ARM vs x86 server architecture is unverified (not exposed in Runtime Admin at either level); x86 loses deployability after 31 Jan 2027. | Low | Confirm via the MRT Admin API or Salesforce Support. Independent of topology, but worth closing while attention is on the platform. | Integration / Platform | --- ## 8. Decision Record | Date | Decision Maker | Decision | Outcome / Rationale | | ------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 12 Aug | Marcel Angelo Navarro (author) | Scope this TSD to two options rather than three. | The originating ticket's "middle option (single modular app)" is not a distinct topology; it is Option A correctly implemented, so it is specified in §5 instead of §3. | | 12 Aug | Marcel Angelo Navarro (author) | State the as-is isolation position from measurement rather than from the ticket text or existing documentation. | The ticket described per-origin pooling as already in place; the pools are in fact imported nowhere and no `fetch` passes a `dispatcher`. Measurement then showed network-level isolation nonetheless exists, supplied by Node's defaults rather than by those pools, while limits, timeouts, error boundaries and observed promises do not. Recorded in §1.2 and §5.3. | | _TBC_ | Tim Lavelle (Technical Lead) | TSD approved for implementation | _Pending review._ | ### Sign-off | Role | Name | Date | Status | | --------------------------- | --------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------- | | Author | Marcel Angelo Navarro | 13 Aug 2026 | Submitted | | Technical Lead / Reviewer | Tim Lavelle | _TBC_ | _Approved / Changes Required_ | --- ## References - Jira: SFCC-681 (this spike) · SFCC-237 (origin, closed at Sprint 2 rollover) · SFCC-1 (parent epic) · SFCC-122 (MRT API capabilities spike: what MRT can *consume*) - [Managed Runtime Overview](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/mrt-overview.html) · [Managed Runtime Administration](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/managed-runtime-administration.html) · [Managed Runtime API](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/references/mrt-admin) - B2C Commerce Headless Integration for ISV Partners: Overview & FAQ (Salesforce, Apr 2026) - Confluence: Technical Solution Design, PWA (256835585) §12.1 Blast-Radius Containment, §14 CI/CD · 05.6 Environment Details (285540356) · TSD Template (352419841) - Repo: `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` · `overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts` · `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5, §9, §9.3 and §12.1 · `.docs/architecture.md` > Blast-Radius Mitigation · AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4 · `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md` - API specifications: [SCAPI](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/commerce-api/references/) · [OCAPI](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/b2c-commerce/references/) · [Script API](https://salesforcecommercecloud.github.io/b2c-dev-doc/) · [Einstein API](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/einstein-api/references/)

input.title: TSD-SFCC-681: MRT Application Topology (Single vs Per-Integration)
input.version_comment: Formatting only: code block language, spacing in §5.2, page icon. No content change.
input.content:
## Document Information | Field | Value | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Document ID** | TSD-SFCC-681 | | **Author(s)** | Marcel Angelo Navarro, Squad A / Frontend Development Lead | | **Reviewer(s)** | Tim Lavelle, Technical Lead | | **Created** | 12 Aug 2026 | | **Version** | v0.1 (Draft) | | **Status** | Draft | | **Related Jira** | SFCC-681 (clones SFCC-237, which was closed at Sprint 2 rollover) | --- ## Version History | Version | Date | Summary of Change | Author | | ------- | ----------- | ----------------- | --------------------- | | v0.1 | 12 Aug 2026 | Initial draft | Marcel Angelo Navarro | --- ## 1. Problem Statement ### 1.1 Context The storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. Integration build-out begins in the coming sprints. ### 1.2 Problem How many MRT applications the storefront deploys, and how integration code is divided across them, has never been decided. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems. Compounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. Seven per-origin connection pools were written to address part of this (`overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`) but are imported nowhere and attached to no request. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection. ### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved - Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy. - The missing error handling persists and compounds. It was found by chance in one of the only three server-side integration touchpoints that exist today, and nothing in the codebase, review process, or CI prevents the same pattern recurring as the remaining systems are built. - Deploy and rollback blast radius stays coupled: a bad change to one integration forces a rollback that also reverts every other integration shipped in the same bundle. - Squad A (FED) and the SFCC squad have no shared written position to build against, risking divergent assumptions about where integration code belongs. ### 1.4 Success Criteria 1. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8). 2. The as-is baseline is verified against the live platform and the codebase rather than assumed, with any inaccuracies in existing documentation identified and raised for correction (§7). 3. The present failure behaviour is demonstrated by reproducible automated tests rather than asserted. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket. 4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question. --- ## 2. Constraints & Assumptions ### 2.1 Constraints | Constraint | Detail | | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. *(Source: MRT Overview, opening constraint statement.)* | | MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. *(Source: MRT Overview, Bundles.)* | | MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. *(Source: MRT Overview, Projects and Organizations.)* Seven environments are in use: the six deployment tiers plus one ad-hoc test environment *(verified in Runtime Admin, 12 Aug 2026)*. | | Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment ("App Server"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** *(Source: MRT Overview, App Server and Rendering constraints.)* | | Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. *(Source: `.docs/prd/regional.md`; `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5 Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture.)* | | Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts share a **single first-party origin** (AU at the root, the other seven path-prefixed); the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. *(Sources: `architecture.md` §Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope; MRT Overview, Environments constraints.)* | | Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual *(Source: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §9 Performance Strategy; summarised in `.docs/architecture.md` > Pre-Build Decisions #3.)* Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. | | Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). | | Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. The verified-session exception does not apply. Any topology or isolation change touches at least one of these. | ### 2.2 Assumptions | Assumption | Risk if Wrong | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | The ~18 systems in `.docs/integration/` remain the integration scope for this decision. | Materially more systems would grow the per-environment variable surface and the number of integration modules the single application carries. | | No in-scope integration requires process-level isolation that in-process module boundaries cannot provide. | If one does, for example a genuinely CPU-bound workload, it must be hosted outside MRT entirely. That is a separate infrastructure decision, not a change to MRT application topology. See §7. | --- ## 3. Options Analysis ### 3.1 Options Summary | Option | Pros | Cons | Viable? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- | | **Option A**: Single MRT application, all integrations in one bundle | + The only model the platform supports, so zero migration cost, since it is the current state.
+ One bundle per environment: the existing deploy pipeline (one workflow per tier: dev, test, sit, uat, stg, prod), version guard and tag promotion already work against it.
+ A single SSR render composes many integrations with no cross-app network hop, protecting LCP.
+ One shared session, cookie and CSP context, which the single-domain 8-storefront session model requires.
+ Isolation is achievable in-process per integration (connection pools, timeouts, error boundaries). | - All integrations share one Node process: no process, memory or event-loop isolation. A CPU-bound operation in any integration blocks every other concurrent request on that process (demonstrated, §6).
- One immutable bundle per environment: rolling back one integration reverts every integration shipped in that bundle.
- One flat environment-variable namespace per environment shared by all integrations; MRT offers no sub-scoping within a project, and project roles are all-or-nothing.
- Isolation must be actively implemented and maintained by convention; nothing in the platform enforces it. | **Yes** | | **Option B**: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain | + Would provide true process-level isolation (memory, event loop, crash domain) per integration.
+ Would provide independent bundle lineage, so one integration could be deployed or rolled back without touching others.
+ Would scope environment variables and project role assignments per integration domain. | - **Not supported by the platform.** MRT hosts only PWA Kit template applications; every project must be a full storefront bundle, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application.
- Salesforce's own ISV integration guidance offers no such pattern.
- Cross-application calls would add a network hop to the SSR path, working directly against LCP ≤ 2s.
- Hostname-per-environment binding conflicts with the single first-party domain session model. | **No** | ### 3.2 Option Detail #### Option A: Single MRT application One PWA Kit project (`zimmermann`) produces one bundle, deployed to one environment per tier. All integration code (proxy routes, token exchange, server-side API calls) lives inside that single Express application, organised as separate modules. It satisfies every constraint in §2 by construction, because it is the model the platform is built around: one bundle per environment, one hostname per environment, one shared session context across all 8 path-prefixed storefronts. Its weakness is that isolation between integrations is a matter of code discipline rather than infrastructure, and must be built deliberately (§5). #### Option B: Dedicated MRT application per integration / domain *(Not viable)* The proposal was that each integration, or each domain grouping of integrations, would be deployed as its own Managed Runtime application, giving each one an independent process, deploy lineage, and credential scope. This was explored in full rather than dismissed, because on paper it addresses precisely the weaknesses of Option A identified above, and because the question was raised specifically to be settled with evidence rather than assumption. It is not viable, for a reason that is architectural rather than a matter of configuration or budget: **MRT will not host it.** Managed Runtime is documented as supporting only applications created from a PWA Kit template, a full React + Express + PWA Kit storefront bundle, and is not a general-purpose Node or microservice hosting platform. An integration's backend cannot be packaged as an MRT application because it is not a storefront. This was confirmed from three independent directions. First, the platform documentation's own constraint statement. Second, Salesforce's own B2C Commerce Headless Integration guidance for partners, which states that every Composable Storefront must have a project created in Runtime Admin and offers exactly three delivery shapes for backend integration logic (an SFCC cartridge, a Node module extending the same PWA Kit server, or an externally-hosted API) with no fourth pattern of a sibling MRT application. Third, firsthand in Runtime Admin: the Create-a-New-Project flow asks only for a name, a project ID, and two environment defaults. There is no application-type field, because the platform assumes every project is a storefront. MRT's genuine multi-project support exists for a different purpose: separating distinct brands or domains, each of which is itself a full storefront, not decomposing one storefront's backend. Even setting the hosting constraint aside, three of Option B's consequences would independently count against it: the literal per-integration form breaches the organisation environment cap; every cross-application call would add a network hop to the SSR path that the LCP budget cannot absorb; and the hostname-per-environment binding is incompatible with the single-domain session model the eight storefronts depend on. The isolation goals behind Option B remain legitimate. They are addressed within Option A in §5, and the one case Option A genuinely cannot serve is recorded as a risk in §7. --- ## 4. Recommended Option & Rationale ### 4.1 Recommended Option **Option A: Single MRT application, with per-integration safeguards in the server-side layer.** ### 4.2 Rationale Option A is recommended because Option B is not available. The decisive factor is not a trade-off between the two but a platform constraint: MRT hosts only PWA Kit storefront bundles, so an integration cannot be deployed as its own MRT application at all. Once that is established, Option A is the only option that satisfies the §2 constraints, and it satisfies them without migration cost because it is the current state. The recommendation is qualified in one important respect. Endorsing Option A is not an endorsement of the status quo, because the status quo includes gaps that are real and demonstrated: integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, three route handlers leave work unobserved, and no upstream call carries a timeout short enough to fail before MRT's own execution ceiling does. Option A is therefore recommended **with safeguards**: one bundle, but with each integration confined to its own module, given its own connection pool with an independent connection cap and timeout budget, wrapped in its own error boundary, and with every route registration observing the promise it starts. These are specified in §5. Adopting Option A without them would settle the topology question while leaving the isolation gap open, which is the state this document exists to close. ### 4.3 Trade-offs Accepted - **Shared-process failure modes remain.** Even fully implemented, in-process module boundaries do not give memory, event-loop, or crash isolation. A synchronous CPU-bound operation in any integration will block every other concurrent request on that process, and no connection pool or configuration prevents it (demonstrated, §6). This is mitigated by a coding rule, not by infrastructure, and is accepted as a permanent property of the chosen topology. - **Coupled deploy and rollback granularity.** One immutable bundle per environment means the unit of deploy and rollback is the whole application. A rollback triggered by one integration reverts every integration in that bundle. Accepted; mitigated only by release discipline and small changes. - **Coarse credential and access scoping.** All integrations' credentials share one flat environment-variable namespace per environment, and MRT project roles are all-or-nothing: anyone who needs deploy or variable access for one integration necessarily has it for all of them. The platform provides no way to scope either within a single project. Accepted; revisit if the team composition changes such that per-integration scoping becomes necessary. - **Isolation depends on convention.** Nothing in the platform or the current CI setup enforces the module boundaries in §5. Accepted, with the mitigation in §7. --- ## 5. Technical Implementation > Scope note: this section specifies the implementation of the chosen option. The work itself is deliberately **not** part of this spike. It is specified here so it can be picked up as its own ticket once §8 is signed off, and because §1.4 cannot be met by a recommendation that leaves the gaps in §1.2 undefined. **Every file listed below is Tier 1**, so the implementing ticket must secure approval before starting. `config/`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and the `overrides/app/ssr/` modules all sit under Runtime & Integration Config, owner Integration / SI Partner (`frozenFiles.md`); `.claude/rules/` sits under Governance, requiring both squad leads and the Integration lead. Two of them, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `config/default.js`, are additionally **absolute** Tier 1 under Hard Rule #4 (§2.1), where the verified-session exception does not apply. At merge time `CODEOWNERS` routes all of these paths to the single `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` team, so there is one review gate but two owner conversations. ### 5.1 High-Level Sequence 1. A shopper request arrives at the MRT environment and is handled by the single Express app in `overrides/app/ssr.js`. 2. The route handler for the relevant surface delegates to an integration module under `overrides/app/ssr/` (one module per integration, as today). 3. The module issues its upstream call via `fetch`, passing the `dispatcher` option bound to **its own** connection pool from `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, so its connection usage is capped independently of every other integration. 4. The pool applies that integration's own `connectTimeout` and `bodyTimeout`, bounding how long a slow upstream can hold a connection, and keeping the request inside MRT's 20s/16s execution ceiling rather than being terminated by it. 5. On success, the module returns typed data to the handler, which renders or responds. 6. **Error path:** if the upstream fails, times out, or returns a non-OK status, the module catches it at its own boundary and converts it to an explicit outcome: an HTTP error response for a dedicated endpoint, or a degraded-but-rendered result for a page surface per the graceful degradation constraint. The rejection **must not** propagate out of the module. 7. **Error path:** the route registration awaits (or explicitly `.catch()`es) the **entire** promise chain it starts, not merely its final call, so no integration failure can become an unobserved floating promise. Three routes do not do this today (§5.2), which is why a Marketing Cloud failure, or an invalid SLAS callback token, currently produces no response at all rather than an error response. ### 5.2 Component / API Changes | File / Endpoint | Change Required | Type | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` | Two origins have hostnames that are still unconfirmed and carry TODOs: `sfccPaymentsPool` and `booxiPool`. Separately, six of the seven pools fall back to a literal placeholder string if their environment variable is unset, so confirm each is populated per tier. Currently defines 7 pools but is imported nowhere. **Also: `undici` is imported here but is not a declared dependency**; it resolves only transitively via `jsdom`. Declaring it requires integration-team approval under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #7, which is a prerequisite for this work, not a detail. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccScapiPool` on the JWKS `fetch` inside `jwksCaching()`, currently a bare global-dispatcher call. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: sfccPaymentsPool` on the `fetch` inside `paymentMetadataHandler()`. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts` | Pass `dispatcher: marketingCloudAuthPool` / `marketingCloudRestPool` on both `fetch` calls inside `sendMarketingCloudEmail()` (token exchange, then email send). **Add a try/catch boundary**; this module currently has none. | Modified | | `overrides/app/ssr.js` is **absolute Tier 1** | Attach a `.catch()` to the **whole promise chain** in the passwordless-login and reset-password callback routes. Neither route observes anything today. Note the chain begins with `validateSlasCallbackToken`, which throws on an invalid or expired token (`slasTokens.ts:33,51`), so a fix that wraps only the inner `sendMagicLinkEmail(...)` call would still leave the auth path failing silently. Also observe the `jwksCaching(...)` call in the JWKS route. Three route registrations currently leave a promise unobserved. | Modified | | `config/default.js` is **Tier 1** | Add a `proxyConfigs` entry per new MRT-mediated integration as each is built (MuleSoft, Google Places, Booxi). Only SCAPI and OCAPI exist today. | Modified | | Runtime Admin, Environment Settings | Matching MRT-side proxy entry per environment. **MRT proxy config is a separate source of truth from the bundle's**; both must be updated together. | Modified | | `.claude/rules/` (new or existing rule file) | Document the integration-module contract in §5.3 so it is enforced at review time. | New | ### 5.3 Data Structures / Interfaces The contract every integration module must satisfy: ```javascript // Each integration owns exactly one pool, and every outbound call uses it. import { mulesoftPool } from './connectionPools'; // 1. All outbound calls pass their own dispatcher. const response = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { /* ... */ }, body: JSON.stringify(payload), dispatcher: mulesoftPool, // per-integration connection cap + timeouts }); // 2. Every module resolves to an explicit outcome. It never throws past its own boundary. type IntegrationResult = | { kind: 'ok'; data: T } | { kind: 'error'; reason: string; status?: number }; // 3. Every route registration observes the promise. app.post(path, (req, res) => { void handler(req, res).catch((err) => { // log, then always respond; never leave the request unanswered }); }); ``` Pool boundaries, origins and connection caps are defined in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 and are deliberately not restated here, to avoid two copies drifting apart. Those caps are derived from expected rather than observed concurrency and should be validated by the Stage load-test pass described in §9.3 of that document. **What the pools add.** Node's `fetch` already creates a separate connection pool per upstream origin by default: it is backed by `undici`, whose `Agent` keys one `Pool` per origin. (Confirmed empirically against the Node 24 runtime rather than by reading a bundled copy, since Node's internal `undici` is not the one resolvable in `node_modules`.) A slow integration therefore does not starve an unrelated one, and that is not what explicit pools are for. What the default does **not** provide is a bound on how many connections a single origin may open, or a response timeout short enough to fail before MRT's execution ceiling. Explicit pools add exactly those two things: a **bound** per origin, so one integration under load cannot consume unbounded sockets or overwhelm its upstream, and a **timeout** that lets the integration fail cleanly and return an error rather than the platform terminating the whole request. ### 5.4 Error Handling & Edge Cases | Scenario | Expected Behaviour | Type | | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | | An integration's upstream returns a non-OK status | The owning module catches it and returns an explicit error outcome. The request receives a response describing the failure, never silence. | Error | | An integration's upstream is slow or unresponsive | Its pool's `bodyTimeout` aborts the call before MRT's 20s/16s ceiling, so the integration returns an explicit error instead of the whole request being terminated by the platform. | Error | | An integration issues a burst of upstream calls | Its own pool caps the concurrent connections, so the burst queues within that integration rather than opening unbounded sockets and pressuring process file descriptors or the upstream itself. | Edge case | | A page surface needs an integration that is unavailable | The page renders without that integration's contribution, per the graceful degradation constraint, except where an explicit error is mandated (checkout). | Edge case | | An integration performs a synchronous CPU-bound operation | **Not preventable by this design.** Every concurrent request on the process blocks for the duration. Prevented only by the coding rule; see §7. | Error | | Contentful (SDK does not expose a `dispatcher` hook) | Connection isolation is not achievable via this pattern; graceful degradation is the mitigation, per the constraint in §2.1. | Edge case | | SLAS callback validation (`jose` fetches the JWKS itself, `slasTokens.ts:38`) | Also outside this pattern: `jose` uses Node's `https.get` rather than `fetch`, so it takes no `dispatcher` (it accepts an `http.Agent` instead). It is not unprotected, however: it applies its own 5s `timeoutDuration` and caches the key set for 10 minutes (`cacheMaxAge`), with a 30s floor on forced reloads after a key miss (`cooldownDuration`), so it is low-frequency and already bounded. Left as-is; revisit only if those defaults prove unsuitable. | Edge case | ### 5.5 Configuration & Environment Notes No new environment variables are introduced by the topology decision itself. Each future integration adds its own credentials to the per-environment variable set, and a matching proxy entry in **both** `config/default.js` and the MRT environment's own proxy configuration. --- ## 6. Testing & Validation ### 6.1 Test Coverage Mapping to §1.4 criterion 3. Three tests exist and pass today (`overrides/app/ssr/blastRadius.test.ts`). The table adds one further row that is deliberately not yet written because it depends on §5, and one recording why no E2E coverage applies. | Test Type | What is Being Tested | Pass Criteria | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Unit / Integration | Asymmetric error handling across the real modules: `sendMagicLinkEmail` and `paymentMetadataHandler` run concurrently against the same upstream failure. | Currently: `sendMagicLinkEmail` rejects out of its module uncaught, while `paymentMetadataHandler` catches its own failure and still responds. After §5: both catch at their own boundary and return an explicit outcome. | | Unit / Integration | The real `ssr.js` call shape (an unobserved floating promise inside a `.then()`) when its integration fails. | Currently: becomes a process-level unhandled rejection and the response object is never written to, so the shopper receives nothing until MRT's ceiling returns a 502. After §5: an explicit response. | | Unit | Event-loop blocking: a synchronous CPU-bound operation alongside an unrelated fast operation. | The fast operation is delayed by the full duration of the blocking work. **This test documents an accepted limitation and is expected to keep passing after §5**; it is not fixed by that work. | | Integration | Once §5 is implemented: that each pool's connection cap is actually enforced under load, and that its timeout fires before MRT's execution ceiling. Note this deliberately does **not** test cross-origin isolation, which §5.3 shows already holds by default. | Concurrency against one origin stays at or below its configured cap; a hung upstream fails through the pool's own timeout and returns an error, rather than running out MRT's 20s/16s ceiling. **Not yet written**; depends on §5. | | E2E / Playwright | Not applicable. | This TSD decides deployment topology and ships no user-facing surface, so there is no user journey to assert. Recorded explicitly rather than omitted. | Performance validation is not duplicated here: per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics are already scheduled for the Stage load-test pass in `tsd-architecture.md` §9.3, and bundle size is already gated in CI. ### 6.2 Regression Risk The topology decision itself changes no code and therefore carries no regression risk. The §5 implementation does, and it is concentrated in two places. First, attaching a `dispatcher` to existing `fetch` calls changes connection behaviour for SLAS token validation, payment metadata, and Marketing Cloud email, all on authentication and checkout paths, so a mis-set cap or timeout would surface as intermittent failures there rather than as an obvious break. The three tests above cover the failure-isolation behaviour but not cap or timeout tuning, which is why the load-test row is listed as required. Second, `overrides/app/ssr.js` is the entry point for every request, so the route-handler change must be verified across all 8 storefronts rather than one. One factor usefully bounds the blast radius of both: a `dispatcher` is passed per call site, so only the four SSR `fetch` calls listed in §5.2 change behaviour. Everything else, including all commerce traffic issued through `commerce-sdk-react`, is untouched by definition. --- ## 7. Risks & Mitigations | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation | Owner | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | §5 is never implemented, leaving Option A endorsed but its isolation gap open, the state this TSD exists to correct. | **High** | Raise the §5 work as its own ticket at sign-off and sequence it **before** the bulk of integration build-out. It is cheap now and grows more expensive per integration added. | Technical Lead / Squad A | | The module contract in §5.3 is not followed by future integrations, since nothing enforces it. The gap was originally introduced this way. | **High** | Document the contract as a rule in `.claude/rules/`, add it to the PR checklist, and consider an ast-grep or lint rule matching a `fetch(` in `overrides/app/ssr/` with no `dispatcher` key. | Squad A | | A future integration proves genuinely CPU-bound or requires process isolation, which Option A cannot provide at any level of implementation quality. | Low | Host that integration's layer **outside** MRT (general-purpose cloud compute, or a vendor-hosted API per Salesforce's Connected App pattern) and call it from the single app over HTTP via its own pool. Reassess if it arises. | Technical Lead | | Connection-pool caps in `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 are derived from expected, not observed, concurrency and may be wrong under real traffic. | Med | Validate against per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics in the Stage load-test pass (§9.3 of that document) and revise before go-live. | Squad A / Integration | | Every file in §5.2 is Tier 1, spanning two owners (Integration / SI Partner, and Governance for `.claude/rules/`), with two of them additionally absolute under Hard Rule #4. Adding `undici` as a declared dependency needs integration-team approval under Hard Rule #7. The implementing ticket can stall awaiting these. | Med | Identify both owner conversations and the dependency approval when raising the ticket, so they run in parallel from the start rather than surfacing one at a time mid-implementation. `CODEOWNERS` routes every path to one team at merge, so the merge gate itself is single. | Technical Lead | | MRT proxy configuration and the bundle's `config/default.js` are independent sources of truth for the same routing and can silently drift. | Med | Treat the pair as a single change unit in the integration checklist; verify both when adding any proxy. | Squad A / Integration | | `tsd-architecture.md` §12.1 justifies the connection pools as preventing one integration from exhausting connections for unrelated origins. Measurement (§5.3) shows Node isolates per origin already, so anyone re-deriving the caps from that rationale starts from a false premise. | Med | Correct the wording in all three copies: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §12.1, `.docs/architecture.md` > Blast-Radius Mitigation (which carries the same sentence and a duplicate of the same 7-pool table), and the published Confluence counterpart. The pools are still required, for the bounding and timeout reasons in §5.3, so no change to this TSD's recommendation. | PWA TSD owner | | ARM vs x86 server architecture is unverified (not exposed in Runtime Admin at either level); x86 loses deployability after 31 Jan 2027. | Low | Confirm via the MRT Admin API or Salesforce Support. Independent of topology, but worth closing while attention is on the platform. | Integration / Platform | --- ## 8. Problem Statement\\n--------------------\\n\\n### 1.1 Context\\n\\nThe storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. That layer currently serves three integration touchpoints: SLAS token validation, payment method metadata, and Marketing Cloud email. Two proxy origins are configured, SCAPI and OCAPI. Approximately 18 external systems are in scope for the programme (`.docs/integration/`), with the remainder still to be built. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off. Because deployment topology determines how code is packaged, deployed, and rolled back, it becomes progressively more expensive to change once integration code exists across many systems.\\n\\nCompounding this, the safeguards that would contain a failing integration are largely absent. Node's `fetch` does isolate connections per upstream origin by default, so one slow integration does not starve another's connections. What is missing sits above that layer: per-origin connection limits and response timeouts are unset, integration modules do not consistently catch their own failures, and three route handlers start work whose outcome nothing observes. All of this is present-state fact, verified in code, and for the in-process failure behaviours by test (§6), not a projection.\\n\\n### 1.3 Impact if Not Solved\\n\\n* Topology is set by accretion rather than decision. Each integration that lands without an agreed position makes the arrangement harder to change, and the decision is effectively made by whoever writes the first proxy.\\n* The missing error handling persists and compounds. A single documented position on how many MRT applications the storefront deploys and how integration code is divided across them, signed off by the Technical Lead (§8).\\n2. The isolation behaviour of the implemented design cannot be demonstrated until §5 ships; that test is specified in §6.1 and is a deliverable of the implementing ticket.\\n4. The position is recorded specifically enough that integration build-out can proceed without re-opening the question.\\n\\n---\\n\\n2. Constraints & Assumptions\\n----------------------------\\n\\n### 2.1 Constraints\\n\\n| Constraint | Detail |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Platform | SFCC B2C Commerce + PWA Kit on Managed Runtime. MRT hosts **only applications created from a PWA Kit template**. It is not general-purpose Node or container hosting. *(Source: MRT Overview, opening constraint statement.)* |\\n| MRT application model | One project has many bundles, but **each environment has exactly one bundle designated as deployed**. A bundle is the entire built application and is immutable once created. *(Source: MRT Overview, Bundles.)* |\\n| MRT organisation limits | Maximum **100 total environments** and **10 production environments** per organisation, raisable only by Salesforce Support. *(Source: MRT Overview, Projects and Organizations.)* Seven environments are in use: the six deployment tiers plus one ad-hoc test environment *(verified in Runtime Admin, 12 Aug 2026)*. |\\n| Execution model | A single Node.js/Express process per environment (\\\"App Server\\\"), serverless and auto-scaling. Hard request-execution ceiling of **20s production / 16s non-production**, after which MRT returns HTTP 502. **Unhandled promise rejections break app rendering.** *(Source: MRT Overview, App Server and Rendering constraints.)* |\\n| Storefront scope | Must work across all **8 storefronts in 6 regions** (AU, UK, US Domestic, US International, EU Domestic, EU International, HK, ME). No single-market workarounds. *(Source: `.docs/prd/regional.md`; `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §5 Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture.)* |\\n| Session and domain model | All 8 storefronts share a **single first-party origin** (AU at the root, the other seven path-prefixed); the `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie depends on this. An MRT environment binds to exactly **one** External Hostname, and a hostname can serve only one environment at a time. *(Sources: `architecture.md` §Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope; MRT Overview, Environments constraints.)* |\\n| Performance | **LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile** is client-mandated and contractual *(Source: `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §9 Performance Strategy; summarised in `.docs/architecture.md` > Pre-Build Decisions #3.)* Any added network hop on the SSR path counts against it. |\\n| Graceful degradation | Each external system must fail independently: one outage must not break a whole page (AGENTS.md > Graceful Degradation). |\\n| Tier 1 change control | `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `overrides/app/ssr.js` and `worker/main.js` are **absolute** Tier 1 under AGENTS.md Hard Rule #4. Problem Statement\\n--------------------\\n\\n### 1.1 Context\\n\\nThe storefront runs on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), where a Node/Express layer performs all server-side work: the SSR render, proxying to upstream APIs, token exchange, and server-side calls to integrated systems. The current arrangement is a default inherited from the PWA Kit scaffold, not a deliberate choice, and it has never been documented or signed off.
